tagline.text: The ruined former Dominican retreat house on Baguio's Dominican Hill

location.label: Location
location.text: Dominican Hill, Dominican-Mirador area (Diplomat Road), Baguio City

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱100–500 (per person, based on city taxi, entry and snacks)

children.text: The Diplomat Hotel is a stone retreat house from the 1910s on Baguio's Dominican Hill. After war, a hotel era and years of neglect, it is now a ruin preserved as a National Historical Site. The interior is closed, but the exterior, the hilltop views and the art events make it a good one-to-two-hour stop.

The Diplomat Hotel is a huge stone building on Dominican Hill, a short way southwest of downtown Baguio. Its official name today is the Dominican Hill Heritage and Nature Park, and it is managed by the Baguio City Environment and Parks Management Office (CEPMO). Many Korean travelers know it first as "Baguio's haunted house," but in daylight it feels more like an open park where families, photographers and students stroll. On a site of about 3 hectares you will find a roofless building, a courtyard with a surviving fountain and a cross on the rooftop, all giving the ruin its distinctive atmosphere.

The building's roots are not in the hotel trade but in a Catholic Dominican retreat house. In 1911, Dominican friars of American and Spanish origin planned a vacation house in Baguio for friars and nuns, and Fr. Roque Ruaño, who also designed the Main Building of the University of Santo Tomas in Manila, was the architect. They bought a hilltop property of about 17 hectares from American residents, began construction in 1913 and inaugurated the building in May 1915. In June 1915 a seminary called Colegio del Santissimo Rosario was set up for tax-exemption purposes, but enrollment was tiny and it closed two years later, according to Wikipedia. The original plans survived in the University of Santo Tomas archives, and conservation experts even built a scale model from them.

The darkest chapter is World War II. Residents fleeing the Japanese took refuge here, but Japanese forces seized the building and used it as a headquarters and last stronghold, and many priests, nuns and refugees are said to have been killed. In April 1945 American bombing partly damaged the right wing, and the building was restored between 1945 and 1947 and returned to the Dominicans. This history later earned the place its reputation as a "ghost magnet." The ghost stories are only tales, however, so it is important to treat the site respectfully as a historic place where victims died.

In 1973, Diplomat Hotels, Inc. bought the building and converted the interior into a 33-room hotel. It was run by Antonio Agapito "Tony" Agpaoa, a Baguio businessman known as a psychic-surgery faith healer. He died in 1987, after which the hotel closed, was looted and abandoned, and the 1990 Luzon earthquake caused further damage. After passing through government ownership, title was transferred to the City of Baguio on April 5, 2005. A 2013 city resolution declared the whole property a historical site, and in September 2014 the National Historical Commission of the Philippines granted it National Historical Site status. In April 2022 it was reported that the National Commission for Culture and the Arts (NCCA) had granted ₱15 million for conservation planning.
The surviving walls and window frames of the roofless, gutted building are the main attraction. Some walls carry paint and graffiti, and the layers of history show up well in photos.
A fountain remains in the courtyard at the center of the building, and a cross stands on the roof. These are the clearest reminders of the days when it was a Dominican retreat house.

The architect who designed the Main Building of the University of Santo Tomas also designed this building. He is said to have had earthquake resistance in mind, so comparing it with the UST Main Building in Manila is interesting.

On the hilltop you can look over Baguio's rooftops and the surrounding mountains. The views are best in the morning once the fog lifts, or near sunset, and access near the roof may be restricted for safety.

Baguio, named a UNESCO Creative City in 2017, has used the site as a base for artists. Events such as the Entacool Festival and the Ibagiw Festival have been held here, and installations such as a bamboo chicken have been placed inside the building.
It was recognized as a National Historical Site in 2014, and a historical marker was installed. After reading the marker, you will see the place as a historic monument rather than a ghost story.

blocks.title: A favorite for filming and shoots

children.text: It has been featured many times in horror specials and is also used for film shoots, wedding photos and cosplay shoots. On weekends you will often run into a shooting crew.

blocks.title: Plans for a cultural hub in a Creative City

children.text: The city has said it wants to bring the site back as a cultural space for artists and craftspeople. According to a 2022 report, drafting the conservation plan takes about six months, the actual restoration needs four to five years, and parts could be in use by around the third year. Keeping the facade intact while adding a parking building and a small restaurant has also been mentioned.

, so ask the driver to use the meter.
Read the signboards and notices at the entrance first. Check on site which areas are currently open and what the entrance fee is.
Walk once around the main building's outer walls and look at the window frames, arches and wall condition. Stay away from spots where stones may fall.
Photograph the courtyard fountain and the rooftop cross, then browse snacks and souvenirs at the stalls on the grounds.
Enjoy the view over the city from the hill, then call a taxi to your next stop.

Start at Dominican Hill. It is quiet in the morning and the light is good for photos.

Have lunch around Session Road.
Climb up to Baguio Cathedral to see its pink twin spires and the staircase.
Move on to Mines View Park or Wright Park to wrap up the day.
Direct buses to Baguio run several times a day from Manila (Cubao in Quezon City, Pasay and elsewhere). The trip takes roughly 5–7 hours depending on traffic.
Fares and timetables differ by bus company and seat class, so check when you book.
If you rent a car, take SCTEX and TPLEX, then Kennon Road or Marcos Highway.
The easiest approach is to take a morning bus rather than a night bus and arrive in daylight.
You can land at Clark International Airport (CRK) and take a bus or van to Baguio.
There are no regular commercial flights to Baguio itself, so overland travel is the norm.

children.text: The easiest way is by taxi. A 2019 travel blog reported paying about
by meter from downtown.
Few Grab drivers are registered, so waits can be long.
Return taxis are said to be fairly easy to find because the site is busy with visitors.
Jeepney routes can change, so ask your accommodation or a local.
Baguio is a highland city at about 1,500 m, so it is cool all year. Since there is not much walking, going in the drier season is more comfortable.
A ruin on a foggy day has even more atmosphere, but stone floors and grass become slippery. Remember that there is almost no roof to shelter from rain in the wet season.

The most convenient place to stay is downtown Baguio near Burnham Park or Session Road. Since you reach Dominican Hill by taxi from downtown, there is no need to book a room near the hill. On weekends and during school holidays rooms fill up quickly, so reserve ahead.

There are simple snack stalls and souvenir shops on and around the grounds for a light bite. For meals you will have the most choice around Session Road and the Baguio City Market. Baguio's famous strawberry products and peanut brittle are also sold downtown.

Around Harrison Road, where the night market is held, and near Burnham Park there are many street snacks and cafes where you can rest after your visit. If local Filipino food is not to your taste, you can also find Korean restaurants and cafes along Session Road. Restaurant hours change often, so check the latest information in a map app before you go. Evenings in a highland city get quite cool, so a light jacket is a good idea.
Go in the morning, when it is quiet and the light is good for photos.
Interior access is often restricted because of falling debris and earthquake damage, so go expecting to see mainly the exterior.
Wear non-slip sneakers and long pants for protection against grass and loose stones.
Current entrance fees and hours differ between sources, so it is best to check with the Baguio City tourism office before you go.
Tell your taxi driver "Diplomat Hotel" or "Dominican Hill" and they will know where to go.
The art installations inside change from time to time, so do not rely on photos of how it once looked.
This is a historic site where war victims died, so avoid shouting or playing ghost games.
If restoration work begins, some areas may close, so check the latest announcements.
The exterior is best seen from the front approach, and if a group shoot is under way, step aside and wait for a moment.
The city may change which areas are open under its conservation plan. Follow the signboards on site over anything written here.
The building is a ruin weakened by earthquakes and neglect. Do not climb inside or onto structures that could collapse.
Some reviews say the city has blocked entry to the building, while others say entry was open. Follow the notices on site for the current rules.
Keep valuables on your person to guard against theft.
Lighting is poor after dark, so it is safer to visit in the daytime.
On rainy days the stone floors are slippery and fog narrows visibility.
Parking is limited, so on weekends it is easier to arrive by taxi or on foot.
